title: One day (109–115)
hookLine: better one day seeing how things arise and pass than a hundred years without seeing it

cards: Some single days stay clearer than whole years. A wedding. A birth.

The day of a diagnosis. A day walking somewhere new, when the light, the food and the faces all seemed to glow. And some years slide by and leave almost nothing behind: the commute, the inbox, the same dinner.
Length and life aren't the same thing. The last verses of chapter eight make that point six times over, then name what makes a day worth more than a century.

teach.h: A HUNDRED YEARS, OR ONE DAY.
teach.b: Verse one hundred ten, in Müller's English: someone may live a hundred years, careless and unrestrained, but “a life of one day is better if a man is virtuous and reflecting.” The next verses repeat the shape.
A hundred years without wisdom, or one day with it. A hundred years idle and weak, or one day of real effort.
Then verse one hundred thirteen: someone may live a hundred years without seeing how things begin and end, but “a life of one day is better if a man sees beginning and end.”

In Pali, udayabbaya: arising and passing away. In the Theravada tradition it names a stage of insight practice: seeing, not just knowing, that every thought, feeling, sound and moment comes up and goes.
The commentary ties this verse to a woman named Patacara. In a single terrible stretch, the story says, she lost her husband, both her children, her parents and her brother.
She came to the Buddha out of her mind with grief, and he calmed her and taught her.
Her own verses, preserved in the collection of the early nuns, describe the turning point: washing her feet, she watched the water run down the slope.
The commentary adds that it ran a short way, then farther, then farther still, and that she saw in it lives ending young, in middle age, and old. That same night, her verses say, her mind was freed.
The chapter's last two verses say the same of seeing the deathless and the highest teaching. Not because the years don't matter.
Because a single day, lived awake, is where seeing happens.

how: In insight meditation, practitioners watch sensations, sounds and thoughts arise and pass away, and the story of the nun Patacara is told as an example of this seeing bringing freedom from grief.

o: a day of clear seeing outweighs a careless century
someday, when the good life finally arrives
a single day set aside each week for rest

games.q: match the pieces of verses one hundred nine to one hundred fifteen.
p: worth less than one day, reflecting
watched water run off her feet

s: these verses say a long life doesn't matter
they say one day lived awake outweighs a hundred years without seeing.
udayabbaya means arising and passing away
in Theravada insight practice, seeing it directly is a named stage.
Patacara's own verses survive in the collection of the early nuns' poems
they describe watching water run off as she washed her feet.

games.q: you're Patacara, washing your feet. you pour water; it runs a short way, then farther, then farther still. what did she see?
o: how lives come and go, like the water.
that it was time to go home.
games.why: in the commentary, the water's short and long runs showed her how beings die young, in middle age or old; her own verses say her mind was freed that night.

practice: Watch one breath begin and end, then the next. Listen for a sound and notice where it starts and where it fades; feel a sensation in the hands or feet arise, change and pass.
Don't hold on to any of it: just watch things come up and go, like water running off onto the ground.
